extracted.intended_audience: critics, teachers and students of poetry; general readers learning to judge and teach poetic works
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and diagnostic criteria for reading, interpreting, judging, and teaching poetry; includes experimental documentation methods (anonymous protocols) and psychological tools to improve critical discrimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making out the plain sense of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The difficulty of making out the plain sense of poetry’ — readers frequently and repeatedly fail to understand poetry as prose sense (overt meaning) and fail to construe it properly; failure affects both statement and expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test by attempting paraphrase/construal as if prose; note that misunderstanding is common even among competent readers; use multiple careful readings (the author records ‘readings’) and return to text when unclear. Treat failure to construe as a primary diagnostic before moral or aesthetic judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensuous apprehension and poetic form (rhythm, metre, sound)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words have form to the mind’s ear and tongue (movement, rhythm). The gulf between immediate perception of form and the reader who must build it up laboriously affects reading profoundly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish inherent rhythm from ascribed rhythm; beware the ‘regularity myth’ and the ‘independence notion’; read aloud; practise slow, close reading of metre and sound; recognise that rhythm goes deeper than the ear and that sound is essential to poetic apprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualisation and imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers differ immensely in capacity to visualise and in the role imagery plays in their mental lives; poets often depend on imagery in ways readers may not share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about judging poetry solely by images it evokes in you; separate poet’s likely imagery from idiosyncratic personal images; diagnose when divergent visualisation causes disagreement between reader and poem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemonic irrelevances
rubrics_metrics.description: Misleading effects of the reader’s being reminded of personal scenes or past emotional reverberations that may have nothing to do with the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when associations are personal mnemonics rather than textually warranted; discount irrelevant intrusions when reconstructing sense and tone; separate autobiographical flash from poem’s communicative content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stock responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Habitual or pre-formed responses that press 'play' when a poem seems to involve familiar views or emotions so that the reader’s reaction may proceed quasi-independently of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise their omnipresence and utility yet their potential to distort; demarcate legitimate stock responses from cases where the stock response replaces engagement with the poem; analyse origins of a stock response (convention, deprivation, moral habit) and adjust judgement accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality and inhibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentimentality: over-facility of emotion (abusive usage includes vagueness, crudity or excessive quantitative emotion). Inhibition is its complement and a positive phenomenon (hardness of heart).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate sentimental responses into senses (vague, crude, quantitative); seek causes (subject choice, conventional metaphors, etc.); consider cures (training, corrective exercises); also recognise necessary inhibition and diagnose its causes and remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrinal adhesions (Doctrine in poetry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry may contain or imply beliefs; readers’ doctrinal commitments (intellectual and emotional) can cause confusion: truth-value of belief may influence perceived worth of poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish intellectual vs emotional assumptions; ask whether the belief is genuinely contained or only seems so to a non-poetical reading; assess sincerity, logic, and adjustment between emotional and intellectual claims; avoid conflating poetic value with literal truth of doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: Sincerity as absence of self-deception, genuineness, spontaneity versus sophistication; sincerity can be viewed as self-completion and is dependent on a fundamental need.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate apparent insincerity carefully (may be appearance only); consider spontaneity and sophistication as separable qualities; note that improvements in sincerity are possible and that poetry can be an exercise in sincerity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figurative language and metaphor handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Causes of misunderstanding include confusion from metre, literalism versus metaphor, mixture in metaphor, personification, poetic liberty, and over-literal reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify literalist errors; distinguish sense-metaphors from emotive-metaphors; be alert to mixed metaphors; use critical comparisons to reveal intended liberties; prefer interpretive flexibility over over-literal construal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense and feeling analysis; verbal techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Four aspects of meaning (sense, feeling, tone, intention) interrelate; there are methods of improving apprehension (verbal means for sense and feeling: dictionary, definition technique, verbal analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply definition technique and dictionary consultation for clarifying sense; use verbal analytic devices (projectile adjectives, precise definitions) to separate sense from feeling; accept comparative helplessness with feeling but train via exercises; practise pre-analytic apprehension checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical presuppositions (mistaking means for ends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectations about technique (how things have been done) can mislead when they become standards; confusing means with ends leads to poor judgement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid judging poetry from outside by technical details alone; beware that a technique’s success in one context does not make it universal; resist the ‘rule of choice’ that turns principles into rigid dogma.

rubrics_metrics.name: General critical preconceptions and dogmas
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior theoretical demands and critical dogmas (conscious or unconscious) intervene between reader and poem and may disable judgement; critical infallibility is a danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat critical theories as protective principles rather than substitutes for discernment; expose critical superstitions and primitive assumptions; use principles cautiously and contextually; maintain humility about applicability of maxims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim of criticism: improvement in communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The one and only goal of critical endeavours is improvement in communication — getting the relevant mental condition intended by the poem so that value-judgement can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise reconstructing the poem’s communicative effect before passing aesthetic judgement; use principles to avoid blunders but not as replacements for achieving the relevant experience; in teaching, demonstrate value through communicated experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation and pedagogical method (protocol experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of anonymized printed sheets of poems given to readers who comment freely in writing (protocols), authorship withheld, multiple readings recorded — a method of field-work in comparative ideology and a technique to discover what readers think and feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve anonymity to secure honest opinion; supply mixed groupings of poems; allow time between readings and collect number of readings as a metric of engagement; use the protocols as primary data for analysing common approaches and errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of psychology in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychology can service criticism by supplying instruments for dissection of opinions, but it can be abused or lead to profanation; psychology helps understand expression vs statement and the mental operations behind utterances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply psychological insights to clarify mental operations (expressions) without overreaching into unwarranted psychoanalytic claims; use psychology to order interpretation and to dissect confusions, but guard against crude or superficial psychological diagnoses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading techniques: slow/close reading, multiple perusals, reading aloud
rubrics_metrics.description: Thorough study requires many readings (protocol-writers often gave four or more) and techniques such as reading aloud and slow, attentive examination of prosody and diction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage multiple sustained readings counted as a single ‘reading’ if they sustain one response; recommend reading aloud to detect sound and rhythm; advocate slow, painstaking analysis rather than rushed responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendations for teaching and critical character (humility, reduced subjectivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions towards remedy include improving the teaching of English, practical suggestions for reading, remedying decline in speech and prose, clearing critical fog, reducing subjectivity, and cultivating humility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In teaching, focus on exercises that build discrimination and construal skills; cultivate humility in critics; combat overconfidence in principles; emphasize training to reduce stock responses and preconceptions.
